football_evidence.question: Can Wisconsin take away UCLA’s big plays?
football_evidence.assessment: Some measured evidence supports EdgeDesk’s lean toward UCLA, and its own breakdown accounts for about 1.0 of the 3.8 points, but not the full gap. It is a research question, not a bet.
supporting: When UCLA has the ball (the line of scrimmage on running plays): UCLA’s offense is stopped at or behind the line on 12.6% of its runs, and Wisconsin’s defense stops 11.1% of opponent runs at or behind the line (FBS average 17.4%).

When Wisconsin has the ball (big plays on the ground): Wisconsin’s offense turns 5.2% of its runs into explosive gains, and UCLA’s defense gives up explosive gains on 3.4% of opponent runs (FBS average 6.6%).
When Wisconsin has the ball (the run game against the run defense): Wisconsin’s offense averages 4.9 yards per carry, and UCLA’s defense allows 3.4 yards per carry (FBS average 5.1).

When Wisconsin has the ball (early downs): Wisconsin’s offense succeeds on 36.8% of its first- and second-down plays, and UCLA’s defense allows success on 33.7% of first- and second-down plays (FBS average 42.8%).
contradicting: When Wisconsin has the ball (pass protection against the pass rush): Wisconsin’s offense has allowed a sack on 2.1% of its dropbacks, and UCLA’s defense sacks the quarterback on 4.8% of opponent dropbacks (FBS average 5.6%).
When UCLA has the ball (the passing game against the pass defense): UCLA’s offense averages 8.3 yards per pass attempt, and Wisconsin’s defense allows 4.7 yards per pass attempt (FBS average 7.5).
Wisconsin comes in on 14 days of rest after an open week; UCLA has had 7 days.
quarterbacks: Nico Iamaleava has completed 71 of 116 passes (61.2%) for 978 yards, 8.4 yards per attempt, 4 touchdowns and 4 interceptions in five games for UCLA, and has been sacked on 7 of 123 dropbacks.
Colton Joseph has completed 80 of 142 passes (56.3%) for 1,132 yards, 8.0 yards per attempt, 9 touchdowns and 4 interceptions in five games for Wisconsin, and has been sacked on 3 of 145 dropbacks.

model: UCLA’s offense has to keep winning on big pass plays: it turns 16.4% of its pass plays into explosive gains, and Wisconsin’s defense gives up explosive gains on 4.0% of opponent pass plays.
UCLA’s defense has to slow Wisconsin in the pass-rush matchup — Wisconsin’s offense has allowed a sack on 2.1% of its dropbacks.
UCLA’s offense has to hold its own through the air against a defense that allows 4.7 yards per pass attempt.
UCLA’s offense has to keep winning at the line of scrimmage: it is stopped at or behind the line on 12.6% of its runs, and Wisconsin’s defense stops 11.1% of opponent runs at or behind the line.
market: Wisconsin’s offense has to keep winning in the pass-rush matchup: it has allowed a sack on 2.1% of its dropbacks, and UCLA’s defense sacks the quarterback on 4.8% of opponent dropbacks.
